response.evidence: By my approximate count, White female applicants were denied in about 17 of roughly 180 applications (~9-10%). This is similar to White male applicants (~22 denials, ~9-10%) and to the dataset's overall denial rate (~10%). Hispanic and some Asian subgroups show comparable or higher denial frequencies. Most White female denials involve clear risk factors: DTI of 50% or higher (about 9 of the 17 were in the '50%-60%' or '>60%' categories), loan amounts exceeding property value or LTV above 95, or very low income (e.g., $22k, $48k, $64k). White female applicants with comparable profiles were usually approved, including several with DTI of 50-60% and LTV of 95-100. A few denials (e.g., DTI 30-36% with LTV 57, or DTI 40 with $473k income) lack an obvious explanation in the data, but they are isolated cases, not a pattern. Limitations: the counts are approximate, no significance test was run, and key underwriting variables such as credit score are missing, so this data cannot prove or rule out discrimination.

These figures are approximate, from a manual review of the rows. White female applicants have roughly 17 denials, a denial rate of about 8-10%. That is broadly in line with the overall denial rate and with other groups. Hispanic and Asian applicants show similar or higher denial counts, and Black applicants have a higher denial rate on a small sample. Most White female denials have clear risk factors: debt-to-income ratios of 50-60% or above 60%, zero or very low reported income (for example, 0 or 35), high loan-to-value ratios of 95% or more on low-value properties, or very small loans on low-value homes. Comparable White female applicants with moderate debt-to-income ratios (below 49%) and typical loan-to-value ratios are overwhelmingly approved. The data shows no consistent pattern of White female applicants being denied when their financial profiles match approved applicants from other groups. Limitations: this is observational data without credit scores or other underwriting variables, so it cannot prove or rule out discrimination.

Counts below are approximate, from a manual review of the rows. About 16 of roughly 170 White female applications were denied (~9%). That is close to the overall denial rate (~8-9%) and to other groups, including White male, Asian, Hispanic and Joint applicants. Most White female denials have clear risk factors: DTI of 50-60% or >60% (e.g., income 23-65k), reported income of 0, LTV above 100% (100.2%, 111.6%), very small loans (35k-55k), or income as low as 22k. A few denials have no obvious financial explanation (e.g., 365k loan at DTI 38; 1.035M loan at DTI 44 and LTV 65). Similar unexplained denials appear in other groups (e.g., Asian male at DTI 38; White joint at DTI 30-36%), so they do not form a pattern specific to White women. Many approved White female applicants have profiles similar to those denied. Limitations: this data lacks credit scores and other underwriting factors and cannot establish causation. It shows no measurable disparity against White female applicants, but it cannot fully rule out discrimination.

These figures come from a manual review of the rows, not an exact computed tally. White Female applicants have roughly 21 denials among about 180-190 applications, a denial rate of about 11%. That is somewhat above the overall rate (about 8%) and the White Male rate (about 8%). However, most White Female denials have clear risk factors in the data: about 6 have DTI of 50%-60% or >60%, several have LTV of 95% or more (including one at 102.7% and one where the loan exceeds the property value), and some have very low income (34k, 68k, 76k). Similar denials appear in other groups, including White Male, Hispanic, and Asian applicants with high DTI or LTV. Applicants with comparable profiles are approved at high rates, and many White Female applicants with DTI of 45-49% and LTV of 80-95% were originated. Only a handful of White Female denials (e.g., DTI 42-49%, LTV 75-80%, adequate income) lack an obvious explanation, and comparable unexplained denials occur for White Male and Joint applicants. The small gap is not clearly separable from differences in DTI, LTV, and income, and the sample is small. So the data does not provide reliable evidence of discrimination against White females. This is an observational dataset without credit scores or other underwriting variables, so it can neither prove nor rule out discrimination.

That is a denial rate of roughly 7%, which is close to the overall rate and lower than that of some other groups, such as Hispanic or Latino applicants. About half of the White female denials had debt-to-income ratios of 50% or higher, and applicants of every race and sex with ratios that high were often denied. A few White female denials had moderate debt-to-income and loan-to-value ratios, such as 655k at 20%-<30% DTI and 50% LTV, or 765k at 30%-<36% DTI and 75% LTV. However, similar unexplained denials also appear for White male, Asian, Hispanic and joint applicants with comparable ratios, so they don't single out White females. Many White female applicants with high debt-to-income or high loan-to-value ratios were approved. The data includes no credit scores, credit history or lender information, so it cannot rule out discrimination entirely. But nothing in it shows White female applicants being treated worse than comparable applicants.
